entries.content:
Healthcare generates huge amounts of data every day, from patient visits and lab results to diagnoses, medications, and medical imaging.

For developers and data engineers building healthcare applications, access to realistic patient data is essential. Whether you are building a healthcare analytics pipeline, testing an Electronic Health Record (EHR) system, or experimenting with machine learning, you need data that reflects how healthcare systems actually work.

But there is a challenge: real patient data is sensitive, highly regulated, and often difficult to access. So how can we develop and test healthcare applications without exposing real patient information? One solution is to generate synthetic healthcare data.

In this tutorial, you will learn how to use Synthea, an open-source synthetic patient generator, to create realistic patient records. We'll generate a population of approximately 100 patients, explore the resulting healthcare datasets using Python, and reconstruct a patient's clinical history.

By the end, you will have your own synthetic healthcare dataset that you can use for learning, testing, and prototyping.

I have also included a companion Jupyter notebook that you can use to explore the generated data with Python, visualize clinical events, and understand a synthetic patient's healthcare journey.

What We'll Cover:

1. What Is Synthetic Healthcare Data?

Synthetic healthcare data is artificially generated information designed to resemble real healthcare records without representing actual patients.

For example, a synthetic patient might have:

  • Demographic information such as age and gender
  • A history of primary care visits
  • Diagnosed medical conditions
  • Lab test results
  • Prescribed medications
  • Procedures and hospital visits

These records are generated using simulation models and predefined rules and not copied from real patient histories.

Synthetic Data vs. De-identified Data

It's important to understand the difference between these two types of data.

De-identified data starts with real patient records and removes or transforms identifying information, such as names, addresses, and other personal identifiers.

Synthetic data, on the other hand, is generated artificially. It doesn't directly represent an actual patient's medical history.

Synthetic data offers another way to create development and testing datasets without relying on actual patient records. But synthetic data isn't automatically statistically representative, clinically accurate, or free from bias.

Why is Synthetic Healthcare Data Useful?

Developers and researchers can use synthetic data in a variety of ways. It lets them develop and test healthcare applications, build data ingestion and transformation pipelines, and experiment with healthcare data models

They can also use it to test interoperability between healthcare systems, prototype analytics and machine learning workflows, and learn more about certain healthcare concepts and data relationships.

For this tutorial, we'll focus on generating structured healthcare data and understanding how the records relate to one another.

2. What Is Synthea?

Synthea is an open-source synthetic patient population simulator developed by MITRE.

Instead of generating random rows of patient information, Synthea simulates patient lifecycles. It models healthcare events over time, including medical conditions, clinical encounters, medications, procedures, and laboratory observations.

For example, a simulated patient might develop a medical condition, visit a healthcare provider, undergo testing, and receive medication. These events become part of that patient's longitudinal health record.

Synthea uses configurable clinical modules and population characteristics to generate these histories.

What Data Can Synthea Generate?

Synthea can generate many types of data, including:

Healthcare dataDescription
PatientsDemographics and patient identifiers
EncountersHospital visits, outpatient consultations, and emergency visits
ConditionsDiagnoses and clinical findings
ObservationsLaboratory results, vital signs, and clinical measurements
MedicationsMedication prescriptions and history
ProceduresClinical procedures and interventions
AllergiesRecorded allergies
ImmunizationsVaccination records
Imaging studiesMedical imaging study metadata
ClaimsHealthcare billing and insurance data

Synthea supports several export formats, including CSV (which is useful for data analysis, SQL databases, and data engineering), HL7 FHIR (a standard for exchanging healthcare information between systems, commonly represented as JSON resources), and C-CDA (an XML-based format for exchanging clinical documents).

We'll use CSV in this tutorial because it's easy to explore with Python and can be imported into relational databases.

3. Prerequisites

Before getting started, you'll need:

  • Java Development Kit (JDK) 17 or newer
  • Git
  • A terminal or command-line environment
  • Python 3, for the exploration section
  • Basic familiarity with CSV files and Python

Synthea recommends supported long-term-support Java versions, such as Java 17 or 25.

I'll demonstrate the commands using macOS, but the same general workflow works on Linux and Windows.

Check Your Java Installation

Open Terminal and run:

java -version

You should see an installed Java version, for example:

openjdk version "17.x.x"

Make sure you're using a JDK rather than only a Java Runtime Environment.

If Java isn't installed, download a compatible JDK before proceeding.

You can also check Git:

git --version

And Python:

python3 --version

4. How to Install Synthea

Let's download the Synthea source code from its official GitHub repository.

Step 1: Clone the Repository

Open your terminal and execute:

git clone https://github.com/synthetichealth/synthea.git

This downloads the Synthea project into a local directory.

Navigate into it:

cd synthea

Step 2: Build the Project

Synthea is written in Java and uses Gradle for building the application.

Run:

./gradlew build

The included Gradle wrapper handles the required Gradle version, so you don't need to install Gradle separately.

The first build may take some time because Gradle needs to download dependencies. When the build completes successfully, you're ready to generate patients.

On Windows, you can use 

gradlew.bat
instead of 
./gradlew
.

Step 3: Check the Available Commands

Run:

./run_synthea -h

This displays the available command-line options.

Some important options are:

ArgumentPurpose
-p
 Target population size
-s
 Random seed
-r
 Simulation reference date
-a
 Patient age range
-g
 Gender filter
-o
 Population overflow setting

You can also modify configuration properties directly through command-line arguments.

We'll use these options in the next step.

5. How to Generate 100 Synthetic Patients

Now we'll generate our first synthetic healthcare population.

From your Synthea directory, execute:

./run_synthea -s 12345 -p 100 \
  --exporter.csv.export=true

Let's understand what the command does.

  • -s 12345
    sets the random seed used during data generation. Using a fixed seed helps make experiments reproducible.
  • -p 100
    requests a population size of 100 patients.
  • --exporter.csv.export=true
    enables the CSV exporter.

This last option is important. Synthea's default configuration doesn't enable CSV export, so running it without this setting may leave you with FHIR files and metadata but no 

csv
directory.

Why Use a Random Seed?

Suppose you're building a data engineering pipeline and repeatedly testing your transformations.

You want your input dataset to remain stable between runs. Using a fixed seed helps achieve this. For stronger reproducibility, also pin the Synthea version and fix the simulation's reference date.

For example, you can add:

-r 20261001

This sets the simulation reference date to October 1, 2026.

Reproducibility also depends on the generator version and configuration, and not every generated field is necessarily invariant across execution environments.

Where Are the Generated Files?

After Synthea finishes, you should see an output directory:

synthea/
│
├── output/
│   ├── csv/
│   ├── fhir/
│   └── metadata/
│
├── src/
├── gradlew
└── run_synthea

The files of interest are inside:

output/csv/

You can list them using:

ls output/csv

Depending on your version and configuration, you'll find files such as:

patients.csv
encounters.csv
conditions.csv
observations.csv
medications.csv
procedures.csv
allergies.csv
immunizations.csv
careplans.csv
imaging_studies.csv
claims.csv
providers.csv
organizations.csv

Each CSV represents a different part of the simulated healthcare ecosystem.

Why Did Synthea Generate More Than 100 Patients?

Here's something interesting I noticed during my experiment. I requested a population of 100, but Synthea generated 115 patient records.

This happens because Synthea normally uses population overflow when generating its target population. The simulation may generate additional people when patients die before the reference date, so the exported records can include more than the requested number.

If you need exactly 100 generated patient records, you can disable overflow:

./run_synthea -s 12345 -p 100 \
  -o false \
  --exporter.csv.export=true

But this changes how the target population is constructed. In particular, the demographics of the surviving population might no longer match the original population targets as closely.

For this tutorial, we'll keep the default behavior because it gives us a more representative example of how Synthea models a population.

6. Understanding the Generated Healthcare Dataset

Before analyzing anything, let's see how much data we've generated.

Run:

wc -l output/csv/*.csv

This counts the number of lines in each CSV file.

Here's a selection from my generated dataset:

FileRecords
patients.csv115
encounters.csv5,985
conditions.csv4,070
observations.csv75,004
medications.csv4,454
procedures.csv16,777
imaging_studies.csv504

These figures come from one simulation run. Your results may differ depending on the version, seed, reference date, and configuration.

Notice something important: we generated a relatively small population, but it produced thousands of clinical events.

That's because a patient may have multiple healthcare encounters over their lifetime, and each encounter can generate several conditions, observations, medications, or procedures.

Understanding the CSV Relationships

Let's look at six important files.

1. patients.csv

Contains demographic and identifying information for each synthetic patient.

Some columns include:

Id
BIRTHDATE
DEATHDATE
GENDER
RACE
ETHNICITY
CITY
STATE

The 

Id
column uniquely identifies a synthetic patient.

2. encounters.csv

Contains information about healthcare visits.

Important columns include:

Id
START
STOP
PATIENT
ENCOUNTERCLASS
DESCRIPTION

An encounter represents an interaction between a patient and the healthcare system. Examples include outpatient visits, emergency encounters, and hospital admissions.

The 

PATIENT
column links each encounter back to a patient in 
patients.csv
.

3. conditions.csv

Contains clinical conditions and diagnoses.

For example:

START
STOP
PATIENT
ENCOUNTER
SYSTEM
CODE
DESCRIPTION

The 

SYSTEM
and 
CODE
columns identify the terminology system and clinical concept.

4. observations.csv

Contains clinical measurements, laboratory results, and other recorded observations.

Some columns include:

DATE
PATIENT
ENCOUNTER
CATEGORY
CODE
DESCRIPTION
VALUE
UNITS
TYPE

Observations might include blood pressure, heart rate, glucose levels, or laboratory test results.

An important detail is that not every observation value is numeric. Some observations contain text.

5. medications.csv

Contains medication-related records associated with patients and encounters.

6. procedures.csv

Contains records of procedures performed during clinical care.

How Are These Files Connected?

Here's the simplified view.

The two key identifiers you'll see frequently are:

  • PATIENT
    : Links a record to a patient.
  • ENCOUNTER
    : Links a clinical event to a healthcare encounter.

These relationships let us reconstruct a longitudinal patient history from multiple tables.

If you want to understand every column, the official Synthea CSV Data Dictionary is a useful reference.

7. How to Explore Synthetic Healthcare Data with Python

Now that we have generated the dataset, let's explore it. We'll use Pandas because it provides a straightforward way to work with structured healthcare data.

Step 1: Install Pandas

From the Synthea directory, create a Python virtual environment:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows, activate the virtual environment using the appropriate script for your shell.

Then install Pandas:

python -m pip install pandas

Step 2: Load the Datasets

Create a file called:

explore_synthea.py

Add the following Python code:

from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

csv_dir = Path("output/csv")

files = [
    "patients",
    "encounters",
    "conditions",
    "observations",
    "medications",
    "procedures",
]

tables = {
    name: pd.read_csv(
        csv_dir / f"{name}.csv",
        low_memory=False
    )
    for name in files
}

for name, df in tables.items():
    print(f"{name}: {len(df):,} records")

Run the script:

python explore_synthea.py

You should see the number of records in each dataset.

We're counting data rows here, so unlike 

wc -l
, the header isn't included.

Step 3: Examine Patient Records

Let's look at the patient table:

patients = tables["patients"]

print(patients.shape)
print(patients.columns.tolist())

We can select a smaller set of columns:

patient_view = patients[
    ["Id", "BIRTHDATE", "GENDER", "CITY", "STATE"]
]

print(patient_view.head())

Although the original data is synthetic, I prefer not to display unnecessary fields such as simulated Social Security numbers, passport numbers, or full addresses. Only use the fields needed for a particular purpose.

Step 4: Explore Encounters

Let's examine the encounters table:

encounters = tables["encounters"]

print(
    encounters[
        ["Id", "PATIENT", "START", "ENCOUNTERCLASS"]
    ].head()
)

We can also examine encounter categories:

print(
    encounters["ENCOUNTERCLASS"].value_counts()
)

This helps us understand the different types of healthcare visits represented in our dataset.

Step 5: Explore Clinical Observations

Let's examine the observations table:

observations = tables["observations"]

print(
    observations[
        ["DESCRIPTION", "VALUE", "UNITS"]
    ].head(10)
)

To see the most frequently recorded observations:

print(
    observations["DESCRIPTION"]
    .value_counts()
    .head(10)
)

This is where healthcare data becomes interesting.

The contains demographic information, but it also contains measurements and clinical events recorded over time.

For healthcare analytics and AI, understanding what each measurement represents is as important as understanding its numerical value.

8. Reconstructing a Patient's Clinical Journey

We've explored the tables independently. But what happens when we want to understand one patient's healthcare history?

A patient might visit a physician several times, receive multiple diagnoses, undergo laboratory tests, and receive medication.

That information is distributed across different CSV files. Let's bring some of it together.

Step 1: Select a Patient

For our example, let's choose the patient with the most recorded encounters.

Add this code to the script:

patient_id = (
    encounters["PATIENT"]
    .value_counts()
    .idxmax()
)

print("Selected patient:", patient_id)

We're selecting this patient because a larger number of visits gives us more events to explore. It doesn't necessarily mean the patient has more severe health conditions.

Step 2: Examine the Patient's Demographics

patient = patients[
    patients["Id"] == patient_id
]

print(
    patient[
        ["BIRTHDATE", "GENDER", "CITY", "STATE"]
    ]
)

Step 3: Find the Patient's Encounters

patient_encounters = encounters[
    encounters["PATIENT"] == patient_id
].copy()

patient_encounters["START"] = pd.to_datetime(
    patient_encounters["START"],
    utc=True
)

patient_encounters = (
    patient_encounters
    .sort_values("START")
)

print(
    patient_encounters[
        ["START", "ENCOUNTERCLASS", "DESCRIPTION"]
    ].head(15)
)

Now we can see the patient's visits in chronological order.

Step 4: Examine Their Conditions

conditions = tables["conditions"]

patient_conditions = conditions[
    conditions["PATIENT"] == patient_id
]

print(
    patient_conditions[
        ["START", "DESCRIPTION"]
    ].sort_values("START").head(15)
)

Step 5: Examine Their Observations

patient_observations = observations[
    observations["PATIENT"] == patient_id
]

print(
    patient_observations[
        ["DATE", "DESCRIPTION", "VALUE", "UNITS"]
    ].sort_values("DATE").tail(15)
)

We have now explored several pieces of one synthetic patient's medical history.

A patient's healthcare journey rarely exists in one table. Understanding it requires connecting different clinical events across time.

A single encounter may have several observations and multiple conditions, so joining both tables without considering their relationships can multiply records unexpectedly.

For this introductory example, examining each event type separately is easier to follow.

9. How to Validate Your Synthetic Healthcare Dataset

Before using any generated dataset, it's good practice to understand its structure and check important assumptions.

Check for Duplicate Patient Identifiers

duplicate_ids = (
    patients["Id"].duplicated().sum()
)

print("Duplicate patient IDs:", duplicate_ids)

Patient identifiers should be unique within 

patients.csv
.

Check Whether Encounters Reference Valid Patients

invalid_encounters = encounters[
    ~encounters["PATIENT"].isin(patients["Id"])
]

print(
    "Encounters referencing unknown patients:",
    len(invalid_encounters)
)

This verifies a basic relational integrity constraint.

Examine Missing Values

print(
    observations.isna().sum()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .head(10)
)

Missing values don't always mean bad data. For example, Synthea can generate quality-of-life observations that aren't associated with a particular encounter. These records may legitimately have an empty 

ENCOUNTER
field.

We should understand why something is missing before deciding whether to remove or replace it. This is especially important when working with healthcare data.

10. Limitations of Synthetic Healthcare Data

Synthetic healthcare data is extremely useful, but it's important to understand what it can and can't represent.

1. Synthetic Data Isn't Real Clinical Evidence

Synthea simulates healthcare events using predefined models and rules.

The resulting data can look realistic, but it shouldn't be assumed to reproduce the full complexity of actual patient populations.

2. Simulated Patterns May Differ from Real-world Patterns

Real healthcare data can contain inconsistencies introduced by clinical workflows, patient behavior, billing practices, interoperability failures, and documentation differences.

Synthetic datasets may not capture all these complexities.

3. Synthetic Data Isn't Automatically Ready for Machine Learning

Generating data is only the first step. Before developing a machine learning model, you may still need to:

  • Validate clinical concepts and coding systems
  • Handle missing and inconsistent data
  • Integrate related datasets
  • Define the prediction target
  • Engineer meaningful features
  • Evaluate data representativeness and potential bias

A model that performs well on synthetic data may not generalize to real clinical settings.

4. The Generated Population Depends on Configuration

Synthea's clinical modules, population characteristics, reference date, and export settings can affect the generated records.

For reproducible experiments, document these settings along with the Synthea version and seed.

11. Conclusion

In this tutorial, we generated a synthetic healthcare population using Synthea and explored the resulting patient records.

You learned how to:

  • Install and configure Synthea
  • Generate a synthetic patient population
  • Export healthcare records as CSV files
  • Understand patients, encounters, conditions, observations, and medications
  • Explore the data using Python and Pandas
  • Reconstruct a synthetic patient's clinical history
  • Perform basic dataset validation

Tools like Synthea give developers a practical way to explore relationships in healthcare data without relying on access to real patient records.

The dataset we have generated can now serve as a starting point for building healthcare data pipelines, testing database designs, experimenting with interoperability standards, and exploring healthcare analytics.

Additional resources

entries.title: How to Scrape Websites in Python with Olostep
entries.summary: Web scraping in Python usually starts with requests and Beautiful Soup. While this works well for static pages, it gets harder when a site loads content with JavaScript, blocks repeated requests, or c
entries.content:
Web scraping in Python usually starts with 

requests
and Beautiful Soup. While this works well for static pages, it gets harder when a site loads content with JavaScript, blocks repeated requests, or changes its markup.

With the Olostep Python SDK, you can pass a URL and get the page back as markdown, HTML or plain text. Olostep renders the JavaScript and manages the browser and proxies for you, and this tutorial walks through your first scrapes. You'll learn how to:

  • Set up the Olostep Python SDK and your API key
  • Scrape a page to markdown
  • Choose between markdown, HTML, and text output
  • Scrape pages that load content with JavaScript
  • Handle errors without stopping a run

All examples here scrape sites built for practice: Books to Scrape and Quotes to Scrape. So you can run every example as it's written here.

Just a note before we start: make sure you always scrape responsibly. The two practice sites let you get started with programmatically scrape the web. On other sites you wish to scrape, you'll need to check and follow their terms of service and 

robots.txt
, collect only public data, and keep your request rate low.

Table of Contents

Prerequisites

  • Python 3.11 to 3.13, which the Olostep SDK requires
  • The Olostep SDK, installed with 
    pip install olostep
  • An Olostep API key from the dashboard. The first 500 credits are free. Also note: the docs price a scrape at 1 credit by default, and the code in this guide makes 4 scrapes, so running all the examples uses about 4 credits.

How to Set Up the Client

All the code in this guide uses one client, and the client needs your API key. The setup below reads the key from the 

OLOSTEP_API_KEY
environment variable and asks for it when the variable is missing, so the key never sits in your code.
import os
from getpass import getpass

from olostep import Olostep

api_key = os.getenv("OLOSTEP_API_KEY") or getpass("Olostep API key: ")
client = Olostep(api_key=api_key)

Let's now parse what each part does:

  • os.getenv("OLOSTEP_API_KEY")
    returns the key when you exported it, and 
    None
    when you didn't.
  • getpass
    prompts for the key and hides what you type, which also works in a notebook such as Google Colab.
  • Olostep(api_key=api_key)
    creates the client that all later code uses.

Run the later snippets in the same session, or paste the setup lines at the top of your file. Each snippet reuses this 

client
. Keep keys out of files you commit.

How to Scrape a Page to Markdown

A scrape takes one URL and returns its content. Markdown is the default choice for most work, because it keeps the headings, lists, and tables of a page and drops the page chrome around them. This code scrapes the Books to Scrape home page.

page = client.scrapes.create(
    url_to_scrape="https://books.toscrape.com/",
    formats=["markdown"],
)

print("Credits used:", page.credits_consumed)
print(page.markdown_content[:400])

Here's what this code does:

  • url_to_scrape
    is the page to read.
  • formats
    lists the outputs you want. Each one arrives as an attribute on the result, such as 
    markdown_content
    .
  • credits_consumed
    reports what the call cost, so you can track spending as you go.
  • The result also carries 
    id
    , 
    url
    , and 
    retrieve_id
    , which identify the stored result.

Output:

Credits used: 1
All products | Books to Scrape - Sandbox           

[Books to Scrape](index.html) We love being scraped!

*   [Home](index.html)
*   All products

*   [Books](catalogue/category/books_1/index.html)
    *   [Travel](catalogue/category/books/travel_2/index.html)
    *   [Mystery](catalogue/category/books/mystery_3/index.html)
    *   [Historical Fiction](catalogue/category/books/historical-fiction_

How to Choose an Output Format

One call can return several formats at once. This code asks for HTML, markdown, and text together and compares their sizes.

page = client.scrapes.create(
    url_to_scrape="https://books.toscrape.com/",
    formats=["html", "markdown", "text"],
)

print("Credits used:       ", page.credits_consumed)
print("HTML characters:    ", len(page.html_content))
print("Markdown characters:", len(page.markdown_content))
print("Text characters:    ", len(page.text_content))

Output:

Credits used:        1
HTML characters:     49846
Markdown characters: 11179
Text characters:     10318

The sizes show why format is important. The HTML carries every tag and attribute, and the markdown carries the content in a fraction of the space. Here's how you can decide which common format to choose:

FormatUse it when
markdown
 You feed the page to an LLM or index it for search
html
 You want to parse the page yourself with BeautifulSoup or a similar library
text
 You need just words with no formatting

For very large pages the SDK also exposes hosted copies of the content, in fields such as 

markdown_hosted_url
.

How to Scrape Pages That Load With JavaScript

Many pages ship an empty container and fill it after the browser runs a script. Quotes to Scrape has a version built to show this: 

https://quotes.toscrape.com/js/
loads its quotes with JavaScript.

Olostep renders the page like a browser would. For content that appears a moment later, 

wait_before_scraping
pauses for the number of milliseconds you pass before it reads the page.
page = client.scrapes.create(
    url_to_scrape="https://quotes.toscrape.com/js/",
    formats=["markdown"],
    wait_before_scraping=2000,
)

print(page.markdown_content[:500])

Output:

Quotes to Scrape  

# [Quotes to Scrape](/)

[Login](/login)

“The world as we have created it is a process of our thinking. It cannot be changed without changing our thinking.”by Albert Einstein

Tags: change deep-thoughts thinking world

“It is our choices, Harry, that show what we truly are, far more than our abilities.”by J.K. Rowling

Tags: abilities choices

“There are only two ways to live your life. One is as though nothing is a miracle. The other is as though everything is a miracle.”by

Some pages need an interaction before the content shows, such as a scroll that triggers more items. The 

actions
argument takes a list of steps that run before the page is read:
page = client.scrapes.create(
    url_to_scrape="https://quotes.toscrape.com/js/",
    formats=["markdown"],
    actions=[
        {"type": "wait", "milliseconds": 1500},
        {"type": "scroll", "direction": "down", "amount": 1000},
    ],
)

The action types are 

wait
, 
click
, 
fill_input
, and 
scroll
. A 
click
takes a CSS 
selector
, and 
fill_input
takes a 
selector
and a 
value
.

How to Handle Errors

Code that reads many pages will meet bad input sooner or later, and one bad URL shouldn't stop the rest. What happens when a scrape can't run? Let's look at the simplest case: a malformed URL.

The problem: one bad URL raises an exception and stops the whole run.

client.scrapes.create(url_to_scrape="not-a-url", formats=["markdown"])

If you try running the above code, you'll get an error like so:

olostep.errors.OlostepClientError_RequestValidationFailed: The request is invalid
Field: url_parsing ('body_params', 'url_to_scrape'), Error: Input should be a valid URL, relative URL without a base

The SDK checks the request before it sends anything, so this failure costs no credits.

So how do you handle invalid URLs and validation errors safely?

When passing an invalid URL to the SDK, a validation error is triggered inside a background thread. Because of how the SDK wraps asynchronous calls synchronously, this background crash prevents the main thread from receiving a value, causing a fallback 

KeyError: 'value'
on the main thread.

To cleanly handle this without crashing your script or cluttering your console with background thread tracebacks, you can:

  1. Override 
    threading.excepthook
    to silence background validation tracebacks.
  2. Catch both 
    Olostep_BaseError
    and 
    KeyError
    on the main thread.
import threading
from olostep import Olostep_BaseError

# 1. Silence background thread traceback noise for validation failures
def custom_thread_excepthook(args):
    if "RequestValidationFailed" in str(args.exc_value) or "ValidationError" in str(args.exc_value):
        return
    threading.__excepthook__(args)

threading.excepthook = custom_thread_excepthook

# 2. Safely capture the error on the main thread
def safe_scrape(url):
    try:
        return client.scrapes.create(url_to_scrape=url, formats=["markdown"])
    except (Olostep_BaseError, KeyError) as error:
        print(f"skipped {url}: OlostepClientError_RequestValidationFailed")
        return None

page = safe_scrape("not-a-url")

Now you should see a similar output message:

Field: url_parsing ('body_params', 'url_to_scrape'), Error: Input should be a valid URL, relative URL without a base
skipped not-a-url: KeyError (likely invalid URL or validation error)


Olostep_BaseError
covers every error the SDK raises on purpose. Its subclasses separate the causes, such as request validation failures, server-side errors, and connection problems. Catch a specific subclass when you want different handling for each.

Conclusion

You now have a working setup for scraping in Python with Olostep. You created a client, scraped a page to markdown, compared output formats, read a JavaScript page and handled errors, all with 

client.scrapes.create
.

Doing the same with other libraries means combining several tools: 

requests
and BeautifulSoup for static pages, Playwright, or Selenium to drive a browser for JavaScript pages, and your own code for proxies and retries. I found using this approach much simpler as it needed far less glue code than combining separate libraries.

Also remember to scrape responsibly. Proceed only after checking a site's terms and 

robots.txt
before you start.

entries.content:
Contracts, invoices, medical reports, and scanned ID cards are often converted to PDF files. And if one of them ends up in the wrong inbox or on a shared drive, anyone can open it.

Adding a password fixes that. A protected PDF is encrypted, so the file is unreadable until someone types the right password.

Most online tools that do this ask you to upload the document first. But that's an odd thing to do with a file you're trying to keep private.

In this tutorial, you'll build a browser-based PDF password protector with JavaScript. You'll open a PDF, choose a password, decide whether people can print, copy or edit it, encrypt the file with AES-256, check the result, and download it. The file never leaves the browser.

The interesting part is that the most popular JavaScript PDF library, PDF-lib, can't encrypt PDFs. So you'll write the encryption yourself with the Web Crypto API, following the PDF 2.0 specification. It's less code than you might expect: about 150 lines.

I built this tool for All In One Tools, where it runs as the Protect PDF tool. This article walks through a simplified version that you can build in three files.

What We'll Cover

What This PDF Protector Does

The finished tool lets you open a PDF by clicking a button or dropping the file on the page. You can type a password that will be needed to open the file (and optionally type a second password for the permissions). You can also choose whether people can print, copy text and images, or edit the file.

The tool also encrypts the PDF with AES-256, checks that the new file really asks for a password and opens it with yours, and lets you rename and download the protected copy.

Through all this, the original file is never changed, and nothing is sent to a server.

How PDF Encryption Works

Before writing our code, it helps to know what a protected PDF looks like inside. You don't need to read the specification, but these five ideas will make the rest of the article easier to follow.

1. The Content is Encrypted, the Structure Isn't

A PDF is a list of numbered objects: dictionaries, arrays, numbers, names, strings and streams (a stream is a block of data, such as the drawing instructions of a page or an image). When a PDF is protected, every string and every stream is encrypted. Numbers, names and the way objects point to each other stay readable, so a PDF reader can still find its way around the file.

2. One Random Key Encrypts Everything

The tool creates a random 256-bit file key and encrypts all strings and streams with it using AES. The password isn't the key.

3. The Password Unlocks the Key

The file stores the file key twice, encrypted with a hash of each password, plus a value that lets a reader check whether a typed password is right. These values live in an encryption dictionary, and the file's trailer points to it with 

/Encrypt
.

4. There Are Two Passwords

  • The user password (the open password) is needed to open the file.
  • The owner password (the permissions password) unlocks the file and lets the owner change what's allowed.

5. Permissions Aren't a Lock

The allowed actions (print, copy, edit) are stored as bits in a number called 

/P
. Good PDF readers obey them, but a program that ignores them can still print or copy once the file is open. The open password is what really protects the content.

PDF has used several encryption methods over the years:

MethodRevisionStatus
RC4 40-bit and 128-bitR2 to R4Old and weak, don't use them for new files
AES-128R4Opens in Acrobat 7 and newer
AES-256R6PDF 2.0 standard, opens in Acrobat X and newer and in all current PDF apps

This tool uses AES-256 (revision 6). It's the strongest option, and it's also the simplest to build, because every object uses the same key.

Let's go through the flow.

From the PDF file:

  • PDF-lib loads the objects
  • random file key (32 bytes)
  • U, UE, O, OE, Perms from the passwords (SHA-2 + AES)
  • every string and stream is encrypted with AES-256
  • /Encrypt dictionary + /ID are added to the trailer
  • the saved PDF is checked with PDF.js and then downloaded

Project Setup

The project is three files and has no build step:

pdf-protector/
├── index.html
├── style.css
└── script.js

Because the Web Crypto API only works in a secure context, open the page from 

https://
or from 
http://localhost
. If you open 
index.html
with a 
file://
path or a plain 
http://
address, 
crypto.subtle
is 
undefined
.

The easiest way to get a local server is:

npx serve .

Then open the address it prints, such as 

http://localhost:3000
.

Libraries and Browser APIs Used

PDF-lib 1.17.1 reads the PDF into objects you can change and writes it back out. It doesn't support encryption, which is why you'll build that part.

PDF.js 3.11.174 is Mozilla's PDF reader. You'll use it to open the protected file, the same way a real reader would, and confirm that it works.

The Web Crypto API is built into every modern browser. It gives you AES encryption, SHA-256/384/512 hashes, and secure random numbers. Never use 

Math.random()
for keys.

Both libraries load from a CDN at the end of 

index.html
:

Creating the HTML Layout

The page has three parts: an upload area, a settings panel with the passwords and permissions, and a result panel. The settings and result panels start hidden.




  
Drop a PDF here or

  
  
  







  
Passwords


  
  

    
    
  

  
Use at least 8 characters.


  
  

  
  

    
    
  

  
Lets you change the restrictions below later. Leave it empty to use a random one.


  
What can people do after opening it?

  
  
  

  
  







  
Your protected PDF is ready

    There are a few details worth pointing out here:

    • The password inputs use 
      autocomplete="new-password"
      , so the browser doesn't fill in a saved login password.
    • The status lines use 
      aria-live="polite"
      , so screen readers announce messages such as "The two passwords are different."
    • The file input is hidden. A regular button opens it, which is easier to style.

    The CSS is ordinary layout and colors, so it isn't covered here. You can copy it from the demo files.

    Opening the PDF

    First, 

    script.js
    takes the classes it needs from the two libraries, points PDF.js to its worker, and keeps the app's state in one object:
    // ---------- Setup ----------
const { PDFDocument, PDFName, PDFNumber, PDFBool, PDFHexString, PDFString,
  PDFDict, PDFArray, PDFRawStream } = PDFLib;

pdfjsLib.GlobalWorkerOptions.workerSrc =
  'https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/pdf.js/3.11.174/pdf.worker.min.js';

const state = {
  file: null,     // the File the user picked
  bytes: null,    // its contents as a Uint8Array
  pages: 0,
  result: null    // the protected PDF as a Uint8Array
};

const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
const uploadArea = $('uploadArea');
const fileInput = $('fileInput');
const fileInfo = $('fileInfo');
const settings = $('settings');
const openPw = $('openPw');
const openPw2 = $('openPw2');
const ownerPw = $('ownerPw');
const strength = $('strength');
const protectBtn = $('protectBtn');
const statusText = $('status');
const result = $('result');
const checks = $('checks');
const fileName = $('fileName');
const downloadBtn = $('downloadBtn');

    The user can pick a file with the button or drop it on the upload area:

    // ---------- Opening the PDF ----------
$('selectBtn').addEventListener('click', () => fileInput.click());
fileInput.addEventListener('change', () => {
  if (fileInput.files[0]) loadFile(fileInput.files[0]);
  fileInput.value = '';
});

uploadArea.addEventListener('dragover', (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  uploadArea.classList.add('dragover');
});
uploadArea.addEventListener('dragleave', () => uploadArea.classList.remove('dragover'));
uploadArea.addEventListener('drop', (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  uploadArea.classList.remove('dragover');
  if (e.dataTransfer.files[0]) loadFile(e.dataTransfer.files[0]);
});

    Setting 

    fileInput.value = ''
    after reading the file lets the user pick the same file again.

    loadFile
    checks that the file is a PDF, reads it into a 
    Uint8Array
    , and tries to load it with PDF-lib:
    async function loadFile(file) {
  const isPdf = file.type === 'application/pdf' || /\.pdf$/i.test(file.name);
  if (!isPdf) {
    fileInfo.textContent = `${file.name} is not a PDF.`;
    return;
  }

  const bytes = new Uint8Array(await file.arrayBuffer());
  try {
    const doc = await PDFDocument.load(bytes, { updateMetadata: false });
    state.file = file;
    state.bytes = bytes;
    state.pages = doc.getPageCount();
  } catch (err) {
    fileInfo.textContent = /encrypted/i.test(err.message)
      ? `${file.name} already has a password. Unlock it first.`
      : `${file.name} could not be read. The file may be damaged.`;
    return;
  }

  fileInfo.textContent = `${file.name}: ${state.pages} page(s), ${formatSize(file.size)}`;
  settings.hidden = false;
  result.hidden = true;
  openPw.focus();
}

function formatSize(n) {
  if (n < 1024) return n + ' B';
  if (n < 1024 * 1024) return (n / 1024).toFixed(1) + ' KB';
  return (n / 1024 / 1024).toFixed(1) + ' MB';
}

    Helpers for Bytes and Web Crypto

    Encryption works on bytes, so you need a few small helpers. 

    concat
    joins byte arrays, 
    randomBytes
    gets secure random bytes, and 
    toHex
    turns bytes into a hex string for PDF-lib:
    // ---------- Byte helpers ----------
function concat(...parts) {
  const out = new Uint8Array(parts.reduce((n, p) => n + p.length, 0));
  let offset = 0;
  for (const p of parts) {
    out.set(p, offset);
    offset += p.length;
  }
  return out;
}

const randomBytes = (n) => crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(n));

function toHex(bytes) {
  return Array.from(bytes, (b) => b.toString(16).padStart(2, '0')).join('');
}

// PDF 2.0 passwords are UTF-8, normalized, and at most 127 bytes long
function passwordBytes(text) {
  return new TextEncoder().encode(text.normalize('NFKC')).slice(0, 127);
}


    passwordBytes
    prepares a password the way PDF 2.0 expects: as UTF-8, at most 127 bytes long. The 
    normalize('NFKC')
    call makes sure that characters which look the same are stored the same way, so for example 
    é
    typed on two different keyboards gives the same bytes. The specification uses a slightly stricter process called SASLprep, but NFKC covers the cases people actually come across.

    Next come the Web Crypto helpers:

    // ---------- Web Crypto helpers ----------
async function digest(algorithm, data) {
  return new Uint8Array(await crypto.subtle.digest(algorithm, data));
}

// AES-CBC with PKCS#7 padding (what PDF uses for strings and streams)
async function aesEncrypt(keyBytes, iv, data) {
  const key = await crypto.subtle.importKey('raw', keyBytes, 'AES-CBC', false, ['encrypt']);
  return new Uint8Array(await crypto.subtle.encrypt({ name: 'AES-CBC', iv }, key, data));
}

// AES-CBC without padding: the input is already a multiple of 16 bytes,
// so we keep the first data.length bytes and drop the extra padding block
async function aesEncryptNoPad(keyBytes, iv, data) {
  return (await aesEncrypt(keyBytes, iv, data)).slice(0, data.length);
}

    Web Crypto's AES-CBC always adds PKCS#7 padding. PDF needs padding for strings and streams, so 

    aesEncrypt
    is perfect for them. But a few values in the encryption dictionary must be encrypted without padding. Their input is always a multiple of 16 bytes, so the first 
    data.length
    bytes of the output are exactly what you need, and 
    aesEncryptNoPad
    simply drops the extra padding block.

    Hashing the Password the PDF 2.0 Way

    AES-256 PDFs don't use a plain SHA-256 of the password. They use a slower hash (Algorithm 2.B in ISO 32000-2) that makes guessing passwords expensive:

    // ---------- The PDF 2.0 password hash ----------
// ISO 32000-2, Algorithm 2.B: SHA-256, then at least 64 rounds of
// AES-128 + SHA-256/384/512 to make guessing passwords slow
async function hashPassword(password, salt, userKey) {
  let k = await digest('SHA-256', concat(password, salt, userKey));
  let e = new Uint8Array([0]);
  let round = 0;

  while (round < 64 || e[e.length - 1] > round - 32) {
    const block = concat(password, k, userKey);
    const k1 = new Uint8Array(block.length * 64);
    for (let i = 0; i < 64; i++) k1.set(block, i * block.length);

    e = await aesEncryptNoPad(k.slice(0, 16), k.slice(16, 32), k1);

    let sum = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < 16; i++) sum += e[i];
    const hash = ['SHA-256', 'SHA-384', 'SHA-512'][sum % 3];
    k = await digest(hash, e);
    round++;
  }
  return k.slice(0, 32);
}

    Here's what happens:

    1. Start with a SHA-256 hash of the password, a salt, and (for the owner password) the 48-byte 
      U
      value.
    2. Repeat the password, the current hash, and the extra data 64 times, and encrypt that block with AES-128. The key and IV come from the current hash.
    3. Add up the first 16 bytes of the result. The remainder after dividing by 3 decides whether the next hash is SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512.
    4. Do this at least 64 times, then keep going until the last byte of the encrypted block is no bigger than the round number minus 32.
    5. The first 32 bytes of the final hash are the result.

    Because the number of rounds and the hash function depend on the data, an attacker can't easily speed this up with special hardware. A browser still finishes it in a few milliseconds.

    Turning Permissions into a Number

    The permissions are stored in 

    /P
    as a 32-bit number, where each bit allows one action:
    // ---------- Permissions ----------
// Bit positions from the PDF specification (bit 1 is the lowest bit)
const PERM = {
  print: 1 << 2,          // bit 3
  modify: 1 << 3,         // bit 4
  copy: 1 << 4,           // bit 5
  annotate: 1 << 5,       // bit 6
  fillForms: 1 << 8,      // bit 9
  accessibility: 1 << 9,  // bit 10
  assemble: 1 << 10,      // bit 11
  printHigh: 1 << 11      // bit 12
};

function permissionFlags({ print, copy, edit }) {
  let p = 0xFFFFF0C0;                    // reserved bits that must be 1
  p |= PERM.accessibility;               // always allow screen readers
  if (print) p |= PERM.print | PERM.printHigh;
  if (copy) p |= PERM.copy;
  if (edit) p |= PERM.modify | PERM.annotate | PERM.fillForms | PERM.assemble;
  return p | 0;                          // as a signed 32-bit number
}

    The starting value 

    0xFFFFF0C0
    sets the bits that the specification says must always be 1. The function then turns on bit 10 (text extraction for accessibility) so screen readers keep working, and adds the bits for each option the user ticked:
    Option in the toolBits turned on
    3 (print) and 12 (high-quality print)
    Copy text and images5
    Edit, comment, and fill forms4, 6, 9 and 11

    The final 

    p | 0
    converts the number to a signed 32-bit integer. With high bits set, it's negative, and that's normal: most PDFs show something like 
    /P -1324
    .

    Building the Encryption Keys

    Now you can build the values that go into the encryption dictionary:

    // ---------- Building the encryption dictionary values ----------
async function makeKeys(userText, ownerText, p) {
  const fileKey = randomBytes(32);       // the key that encrypts the document
  const user = passwordBytes(userText);
  const owner = passwordBytes(ownerText);
  const none = new Uint8Array(0);
  const zeroIv = new Uint8Array(16);

  // U and UE: check the open password and unlock the file key with it
  const uValidation = randomBytes(8);
  const uKeySalt = randomBytes(8);
  const U = concat(await hashPassword(user, uValidation, none), uValidation, uKeySalt);
  const UE = await aesEncryptNoPad(await hashPassword(user, uKeySalt, none), zeroIv, fileKey);

  // O and OE: the same for the permissions password (they also depend on U)
  const oValidation = randomBytes(8);
  const oKeySalt = randomBytes(8);
  const O = concat(await hashPassword(owner, oValidation, U), oValidation, oKeySalt);
  const OE = await aesEncryptNoPad(await hashPassword(owner, oKeySalt, U), zeroIv, fileKey);

  // Perms: the permissions, encrypted with the file key so they can't be edited
  const perms = new Uint8Array(16);
  new DataView(perms.buffer).setInt32(0, p, true);   // little-endian
  perms.set([0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF], 4);
  perms.set([0x54, 0x61, 0x64, 0x62], 8);            // 'T' (encrypt metadata), 'a', 'd', 'b'
  perms.set(randomBytes(4), 12);
  const Perms = await aesEncryptNoPad(fileKey, zeroIv, perms);

  return { fileKey, U, UE, O, OE, Perms };
}

    Let's go through them:

    • fileKey
      is 32 random bytes. It encrypts the whole document.
    • U
      (48 bytes) lets a reader check the user password. It's the password hash plus two 8-byte random salts: a validation salt used to check the password, and a key salt used to unlock the key.
    • UE
      is the file key, encrypted with a hash of the user password and the key salt. When someone types the right password, the reader rebuilds this hash and decrypts the file key.
    • O
      and 
      OE
      do the same for the owner password. Their hashes also include 
      U
      , which ties the two passwords to the same file.
    • Perms
      is the permission number plus a few check bytes, encrypted with the file key. A reader decrypts it and compares it with 
      /P
      , so someone who edits 
      /P
      in a text editor gets caught.

    Two rules from the specification show up here:

    • UE
      , 
      OE
      and 
      Perms
      are encrypted without padding and with an IV of zeros. (
      Perms
      is a single 16-byte block, so AES-CBC with a zero IV gives the same result as the AES-ECB mode the specification describes.)
    • The byte 
      T
      in 
      Perms
      means "the metadata is encrypted too", which must match 
      /EncryptMetadata true
      in the dictionary.

    Encrypting Every String and Stream

    With the file key ready, you can encrypt the document. For AES-256, each string or stream is encrypted with the file key and a new random 16-byte IV, and the IV is stored in front of the encrypted bytes:

    // ---------- Encrypting the objects ----------
// With AES-256 every string and stream is encrypted with the file key
// and a fresh random IV, which is stored in front of the encrypted data
async function encryptData(fileKey, data) {
  const iv = randomBytes(16);
  return concat(iv, await aesEncrypt(fileKey, iv, data));
}

async function encryptStrings(value, fileKey) {
  if (value instanceof PDFDict) {
    for (const [key, item] of value.entries()) {
      const replacement = await encryptValue(item, fileKey);
      if (replacement) value.set(key, replacement);
    }
  } else if (value instanceof PDFArray) {
    for (let i = 0; i < value.size(); i++) {
      const replacement = await encryptValue(value.get(i), fileKey);
      if (replacement) value.set(i, replacement);
    }
  }
}

async function encryptValue(item, fileKey) {
  if (item instanceof PDFString || item instanceof PDFHexString) {
    return PDFHexString.of(toHex(await encryptData(fileKey, item.asBytes())));
  }
  await encryptStrings(item, fileKey);   // nested dictionaries and arrays
  return null;
}

async function encryptObjects(context, fileKey) {
  const objects = context.enumerateIndirectObjects();
  for (const [ref, object] of objects) {
    if (object instanceof PDFRawStream) {
      const type = object.dict.get(PDFName.of('Type'));
      if (type === PDFName.of('XRef')) {     // old cross-reference streams
        context.delete(ref);
        continue;
      }
      await encryptStrings(object.dict, fileKey);
      const data = await encryptData(fileKey, object.contents);
      context.assign(ref, PDFRawStream.of(object.dict, data));
    } else {
      await encryptStrings(object, fileKey);
    }
  }
}


    encryptObjects
    goes through every object in the file:
    • Streams (
      PDFRawStream
      ): their data is replaced with the encrypted version. PDF-lib updates the 
      /Length
      entry for you when it saves.
    • Dictionaries and arrays: 
      encryptStrings
      walks through them and replaces every string with an encrypted hex string. Nested dictionaries and arrays are handled by calling the function again.
    • Cross-reference streams (
      /Type /XRef
      ) are deleted. They describe where objects sit in the old file, PDF-lib writes a new cross-reference table anyway, and they must never be encrypted.

    PDF-lib has two string types: 

    PDFString
    for literal strings like 
    (Hello)
    and 
    PDFHexString
    for hex strings like 
    <48656C6C6F>
    . Both have an 
    asBytes()
    method that returns the real bytes, which is what you encrypt.

    The stream data is encrypted as it is in the file, which is usually already compressed. That's the correct order: a reader decrypts first, then decompresses.

    Writing the Protected PDF

    protectPdf
    puts it all together:
    // ---------- Protecting the PDF ----------
async function protectPdf(bytes, options) {
  const doc = await PDFDocument.load(bytes, { updateMetadata: false });
  const context = doc.context;

  const p = permissionFlags(options);
  const ownerText = options.ownerPw || toHex(randomBytes(16));
  const keys = await makeKeys(options.openPw, ownerText, p);

  // 1. Encrypt every string and stream that is already in the file
  await encryptObjects(context, keys.fileKey);

  // 2. Add the encryption dictionary (it must NOT be encrypted itself)
  const hex = (b) => PDFHexString.of(toHex(b));
  const stdCF = context.obj({ AuthEvent: 'DocOpen', CFM: 'AESV3', Length: 32 });
  const encrypt = context.obj({
    Filter: 'Standard',
    V: 5,
    R: 6,
    Length: 256,
    CF: context.obj({ StdCF: stdCF }),
    StmF: 'StdCF',
    StrF: 'StdCF',
    P: PDFNumber.of(p),
    EncryptMetadata: PDFBool.True
  });
  encrypt.set(PDFName.of('U'), hex(keys.U));
  encrypt.set(PDFName.of('UE'), hex(keys.UE));
  encrypt.set(PDFName.of('O'), hex(keys.O));
  encrypt.set(PDFName.of('OE'), hex(keys.OE));
  encrypt.set(PDFName.of('Perms'), hex(keys.Perms));

  // 3. Point the trailer at it and give the file an ID
  context.trailerInfo.Encrypt = context.register(encrypt);
  const id = hex(randomBytes(16));
  context.trailerInfo.ID = context.obj([id, id]);

  // Object streams would hide objects from step 1, so write plain objects
  return doc.save({ useObjectStreams: false });
}

    The steps are:

    1. Encrypt the existing objects: This must happen before you add the encryption dictionary, because the dictionary itself must stay readable.
    2. Create the encryption dictionary: 
      context.obj()
      turns plain strings into PDF names, so 
      Filter: 'Standard'
      becomes 
      /Filter /Standard
      . 
      V 5
      and 
      R 6
      mean AES-256 from PDF 2.0, and the crypt filter 
      StdCF
      with 
      CFM AESV3
      tells the reader to use AES-256 for both streams (
      StmF
      ) and strings (
      StrF
      ).
    3. Update the trailer: The trailer gets an 
      /Encrypt
      reference and a new 
      /ID
      . PDF-lib writes 
      trailerInfo
      into the trailer for you, and it doesn't encrypt the ID.

    If the user leaves the permissions password empty, the tool uses 16 random bytes as the owner password. Nobody knows it, so nobody can lift the restrictions. (If you used an empty owner password instead, any PDF program could remove them.)

    Finally, the file is saved with 

    useObjectStreams: false
    . An object stream packs many objects into one compressed stream. Strings inside an object stream must not be encrypted on their own, because the whole stream is encrypted. You already encrypted every string individually, so writing plain objects keeps the file correct.

    Here's what the encryption dictionary looks like in the saved file:

    <<
/Filter /Standard /V 5 /R 6 /Length 256
/CF << /StdCF << /AuthEvent /DocOpen /CFM /AESV3 /Length 32 >> >>
/StmF /StdCF /StrF /StdCF
/P -1324 /EncryptMetadata true
/U <...48 bytes...> /UE <...32 bytes...>
/O <...48 bytes...> /OE <...32 bytes...>
/Perms <...16 bytes...>
>>

    Checking the Result with PDF.js

    Encryption bugs are easy to make and hard to notice. A file might open in one reader and fail in another, or it might not be encrypted at all. So the tool opens its own output with PDF.js before offering the download:

    // ---------- Checking the result with PDF.js ----------
async function verify(bytes, password) {
  const results = [];

  // 1. Without a password, PDF.js must ask for one
  try {
    const doc = await pdfjsLib.getDocument({ data: bytes.slice() }).promise;
    await doc.destroy();
    results.push([false, 'The file opened without a password']);
  } catch (err) {
    results.push([err.name === 'PasswordException', 'Asks for a password when opened']);
  }

  // 2. With the password, it must open and have every page
  try {
    const doc = await pdfjsLib.getDocument({ data: bytes.slice(), password }).promise;
    results.push([doc.numPages === state.pages, `Opens with your password (${doc.numPages} page(s))`]);
    await doc.destroy();
  } catch (err) {
    results.push([false, 'Could not open it with your password']);
  }
  return results;
}

    There are two checks:

    1. Opening the file without a password must fail with a 
      PasswordException
      . If it opens, the file isn't protected.
    2. Opening it with the password must work, and it must have the same number of pages as the original.

    bytes.slice()
    passes a copy, because PDF.js moves the buffer to its worker and the original array would become empty.

    Performance Tips

    There are a few things you can do to make sure the tool performs well.

    First, process objects one at a time. The code 

    await
    s each encryption in turn. That keeps memory use low, because only one stream is copied at a time. For files with thousands of small objects you can encrypt in batches of, say, 50 with 
    Promise.all
    to go faster.

    Second, expect the file to grow a little. Each string and stream gains a 16-byte IV and up to 16 bytes of padding, and saving without object streams makes the cross-reference table bigger. A 4 KB file might become 8 KB, while a 5 MB file grows by only a few kilobytes.

    Next, don't encrypt twice for the check. The tool verifies the exact bytes it's going to download. Don't run 

    protectPdf
    again for the download, or the file will get a new random key and the check will no longer apply to it.

    Finally, release memory after big files. Call 

    doc.destroy()
    on PDF.js documents when you're done, as 
    verify
    does. Otherwise the worker keeps the parsed file in memory.

    Common Mistakes

    There are also a few things to avoid when you're building this tool.

    First, don't open the page over plain 

    http://
    . 
    crypto.subtle
    only exists in secure contexts. On 
    http://example.com
    or a 
    file://
    path, the code fails with "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'digest')". Use 
    https://
    or 
    localhost
    .

    Don't use 

    Math.random()
    for keys or salts. It isn't designed for security, and its output can be predicted. Always use 
    crypto.getRandomValues()
    .

    You also shouldn't encrypt the encryption dictionary. If the 

    /U
    , 
    /O
    or 
    /Perms
    strings get encrypted, no reader can check a password. Encrypt the document first, then add the dictionary.

    Avoid saving with object streams. PDF-lib saves with object streams by default. With encryption, strings inside them would be encrypted twice. Pass 

    useObjectStreams: false
    .

    Also, don't forget 

    slice()
    when passing bytes to PDF.js. PDF.js transfers the buffer to its worker. Afterwards your original 
    Uint8Array
    is empty, and the download is a 0-byte file.

    Don't treat permissions as security. Restricting printing and copying is useful for honest readers, but it isn't protection. If the content must stay private, the open password is what matters.

    Don't protect a digitally signed PDF. Encrypting changes every byte that the signature covers, so the signature becomes invalid. Add the password first, then sign the protected file.

    And finally, make sure you and your users don't lose the password. With AES-256 there's no back door and no "forgot password" button. Tell your users to store the password somewhere safe.

entries.content:
Data structures such as arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps, and graphs determine how a program stores data and how fast it can search, insert, and remove items. Big O notation describes how the number of steps grows as the input grows.

We just published a course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel that will teach you data structures and algorithms in Python, with every topic explained through custom animations and visualizations alongside Python code examples. This course is taught by Javid Bodurov.

The course is for beginners and only assumes the basics of Python: variables, loops, functions, and lists. You build each structure yourself, then compare it with tools Python already has, such as dict, set, deque, and heapq.

In this course, you will learn:

  • Big O, Arrays & Linked Lists

    How to measure how a program's steps grow, how data lives in memory, and why inserting at the head of a linked list changes only two pointers.
  • Stacks, Queues & Hash Tables

    How to solve the balanced brackets problem with a stack, use deque for fast queues, and handle collisions in a hash table.
  • Trees, Heaps & Graphs

    How binary search trees keep values ordered, how a heap gives you the smallest value first, and how breadth first search, depth first search, and Dijkstra's algorithm work on graphs.
  • Recursion, Searching & Sorting

    How memoization fixes a slow recursive Fibonacci, how binary search works on a sorted list, and how bubble, selection, insertion, merge, and quick sort compare.
  • Problem-Solving Patterns & Interview Problems

    How to recognize patterns such as two pointers and sliding windows, then bring everything together to approach coding interview problems.

Watch the full course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel (2.5-hour watch).
